On the ground states of the Ostrovskyi equation and their stabilityThanks:  Posukhovskyi is partially supported from a graduate fellowship by NSF-DMS under grant # 1614734. Stefanov is partially supported by NSF-DMS under grants # 1614734 and # 1908626.

Iurii Posukhovskyi Address:  Department of Mathematics, University of Kansas, 1460 Jayhawk Boulevard, Lawrence KS 66045–7523, USA Email address: i.posukhovskyi@ku.edu and Atanas Stefanov Address:  Department of Mathematics, University of Kansas, 1460 Jayhawk Boulevard, Lawrence KS 66045–7523, USA Email address: stefanov@ku.edu
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

The Ostrovskyi (Ostrovskyi-Vakhnenko/short pulse) equations are ubiquitous models in mathematical physics. They describe water waves under the action of a Coriolis force as well as the amplitude of a “short” pulse in an optical fiber.

In this paper, we rigorously construct ground traveling waves for these models as minimizers of the Hamiltonian functional for any fixed L2L^{2} norm. The existence argument proceeds via the method of compensated compactness, but it requires surprisingly detailed Fourier analysis arguments to rule out the non-vanishing of the limits of the minimizing sequences. We show that all of these waves are weakly non-degenerate and spectrally stable.

Key words and phrases: 
ground states, Ostrovskyi equation, stability
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 35Q55, 35 Q51, 35 L 60

1. Introduction and main results

The Ostrovskyi model, which is ubiquitous in the modern water waves theory, is given by,

(1.1) (ut−ux​x​x−(u2)x)x=u.(u_{t}-u_{xxx}-(u^{2})_{x})_{x}=u.

The related, generalized Ostrovskyi/Vakhnenko/short pulse equation is the corresponding equation with cubic nonlinearity

(1.2) (ut−ux​x​x−(u3)x)x=u.(u_{t}-u_{xxx}-(u^{3})_{x})_{x}=u.

These models have attracted a lot of attention in the last thirty years, as models of water waves under the action of a Coriolis force, [14, 15, 2], as well as the amplitude of a “short” pulse in an optical fiber, [17]. In this paper, we shall be interested in the dynamics of a family of problems, which contains these two. More specifically, we consider the following generalized Ostrovskyi models

(1.3) (ut−ux​x​x−(|u|p)x)x=u\displaystyle\left(u_{t}-u_{xxx}-(|u|^{p})_{x}\right)_{x}=u
(1.4) (ut−ux​x​x−(|u|p−1​u)x)x=u\displaystyle\left(u_{t}-u_{xxx}-(|u|^{p-1}u)_{x}\right)_{x}=u

Clearly, (1.3), in the case p=2p=2 is nothing but (1.1), while (1.4), for p=3p=3 is (1.2). Let us comment on the seemingly more general form of the equations that appear in other publications,

(1.5) (ut−β​ux​x​x−σ​(|u|p)x)x=γ​u,(x,t)∈ℝ×ℝ\left(u_{t}-\beta u_{xxx}-\sigma(|u|^{p})_{x}\right)_{x}=\gamma u,\ \ (x,t)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}

Using the scaling transformations t→a​t,x→b​x,u→c​ut\to at,x\to bx,u\to cu, we obtain the equivalent problem

(ut−β​b3a​ux​x​x−σ​b​|c|p−2​ca​(|u|p)x)x=γa​b​u\left(u_{t}-\frac{\beta b^{3}}{a}u_{xxx}-\frac{\sigma b|c|^{p-2}c}{a}(|u|^{p})_{x}\right)_{x}=\frac{\gamma}{ab}u

which means that by choosing a,b,ca,b,c appropriately, we may scale all the coefficients to plus or minus one, just as in (1.3). In addition, by a judicious choice of the signs of a,b,ca,b,c, one concludes that all systems in the form (1.5) reduce to

(ut−ϵ1​s​g​n​(β)​ux​x​x−ϵ2​(|u|p)x)x=s​g​n​(γ)​ϵ1​u(u_{t}-\epsilon_{1}sgn(\beta)u_{xxx}-\epsilon_{2}(|u|^{p})_{x})_{x}=sgn(\gamma)\epsilon_{1}u

where ϵ1,ϵ2∈{−1,1}\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}\in\{-1,1\}. In this work, we stick to the case11 1 It is well-known that solitary waves do not exists in the case when s​g​n​(β)≠s​g​n​(γ)sgn(\beta)\neq sgn(\gamma) s​g​n​(β)=s​g​n​(γ)sgn(\beta)=sgn(\gamma). In this case, an appropriate further rescale leads us to

(1.6) (ut−ux​x​x−ϵ​(|u|p)x)x=u.(u_{t}-u_{xxx}-\epsilon(|u|^{p})_{x})_{x}=u.

Thus, our model, (1.3), covers the cases for which ϵ=1\epsilon=1.

Let us record another, mostly equivalent formulation of (1.3) and (1.4). Using u=vxu=v_{x} in (1.3) and integrating once (by tacitly assuming that v,vxv,v_{x} vanishes at ±∞\pm\infty), we get

(1.7) (vt−vx​x​x−(|vx|p))x=v,(vt−vx​x​x−(|vx|p−1​vx))x=v.\displaystyle\begin{split}(v_{t}-v_{xxx}-(|v_{x}|^{p}))_{x}=v,\\ (v_{t}-v_{xxx}-(|v_{x}|^{p-1}v_{x}))_{x}=v.\end{split}

Regarding local and global well-posedness for these models, most of the theory has been developed for standard quadratic and cubic models (1.1), [3, 17, 19, 20, 13, 16]. Extensive further references to earlier works can be found in [19, 20]. Break up in finite time is shown in various situations in [10].

The main purpose of this paper is the study of traveling wave solutions, namely functions in the form ϕ⁡(x−ω​t)\phi(x-\omega t). More specifically, plugging in this ansatz in (1.7) turns it into the profile equation

(1.8) ϕ′′′′+ω​ϕ′′+ϕ+(|ϕ′|p)′=0,ϕ′′′′+ω​ϕ′′+ϕ+(|ϕ′|p−1​ϕ′)′=0.\displaystyle\begin{split}\phi^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}+\omega\phi^{\prime\prime}+\phi+(|\phi^{\prime}|^{p})^{\prime}=0,\\ \phi^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}+\omega\phi^{\prime\prime}+\phi+(|\phi^{\prime}|^{p-1}\phi^{\prime})^{\prime}=0.\end{split}

These are fourth order nonlinear ODE’s, for which there is not very well-developed theory. In particular, for non-integer values of pp, existence has been proved by variational methods, [6, 7, 5], so that (1.8) is an Euler-Lagrange equation for these constrained minimizers. Regarding uniqueness, which is well-known to be a hard issue22 2 even for second order problems of this type is only known in the case p=2p=2. This is the main result of [21], where it is shown that localized solutions are unique, together with some asymptotic decay properties of ϕ\phi and its derivatives. Note that the result obtained there rely heavily on the quadratic nonlinearity as well as the precise structure of the equation. We provide an independent analysis of the elliptic profile equations, (1.8) and we also compute, what we believe, are the sharp spatial exponential rate of decay, see Proposition 2 below.

Our approach to (1.8) is variational, but rather different than the works [5, 6, 7]. More precisely, Levandosky and Liu construct their waves as minimizers of energy, subject to a fixed Lp+1L^{p+1} norm. This method allows for a construction of waves for any power of p>1p>1. As shown therein, some of these waves, for large enough pp, are spectrally unstable. On the other hand, our goal is to construct the so-called normalized waves - that is, we construct the waves to minimize energy, by keeping their L2L^{2} norm fixed. As we show later in the paper, see Theorem 1, this imposes restrictions on pp, but the result is that all of these waves are necessarily spectrally stable. We state our results below, starting with the existence, and then proceeding onto the stability.

1.2. Stability results

We start by describing in detail the state of the art, regarding the stability of the Ostrovsky waves. For the reduced Ostrovsky case, that is the model without the dispersive term ux​x​xu_{xxx} and with quadratic or cubic non-linearities, much is known, as the model is in some sense completely integrable. A full description of its periodic waves as well their stability can be found in the recent papers, [1, 4].

For the full Ostrovsky model under consideration, Liu and Ohta, [11] and by a slightly different method, Liu, [9] have established the orbital stability for the classical Ostrovsky’s equation (i.e. p=2p=2) for large speeds. Another, set stability result, sometimes referred to as weak orbital stability, is given in [12]. In the works, [6], [7], Levandosky and Liu have constructed the waves for the generalized problems and they have shown that their orbital stability is reduced to the convexity of certain scalar functions, a la Grillakis-Shatah-Strauss. In [5], Levandosky obtained rigorously the orbital stability of the waves near some bifurcation points. In addition, he has launched an impressive numerical study, which was our main motivation for this work.

In order to state our stability results, we need to introduce the linearized operators as well. Namely, for a traveling wave ϕ\phi, solving either one of the elliptic equations in (1.8), set u⁡(t,x)=ϕ⁡(x−ω​t)+v⁡(t,x−ω​t)u(t,x)=\phi(x-\omega t)+v(t,x-\omega t) into (1.7). After ignoring O⁡(v2)O(v^{2}) terms we get

(1.14) (vx)t−vx​x​x​x−ω​vx​x−v−p​(|ϕ′|p−2​ϕ′​vx)x=0.(v_{x})_{t}-v_{xxxx}-\omega v_{xx}-v-p(|\phi^{\prime}|^{p-2}\phi^{\prime}v_{x})_{x}=0.

Setting the stability ansatz v⁡(t,x)=et​μ​z​(x)v(t,x)=e^{t\mu}z(x) in (1.14), we obtain the eigenvalue problem in the form

(1.15) L+z=μ∂xz,L+=∂x​x​x​x+ω∂x​x+1+p∂x(|ϕ′|p−2ϕ′∂x(⋅)).L_{+}z=\mu\partial_{x}z,\ \ L_{+}=\partial_{xxxx}+\omega\partial_{xx}+1+p\partial_{x}(|\phi^{\prime}|^{p-2}\phi^{\prime}\partial_{x}(\cdot)).

Clearly, (L+,D⁡(L+))=H4​(ℝ)(L_{+},D(L_{+}))=H^{4}(\mathbb{R}) is unbounded, but self-adjoint operator on L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}). Spectral instability here is understood as the existence of a non-trivial pair (μ,z):ℜ⁡μ>0,z≠0,z∈D⁡(L+)(\mu,z):\Re\mu>0,z\neq 0,z\in D(L_{+}), so that (1.15) is satisfied. Spectral stability means non-existence of such pair.

The eigenvalue problem (1.15) is a non-standard one, although problems in this form were recently considered in the literature. An equivalent formulation, which is technically more convenient for our approach is the following: write L+=−∂xℒ+∂xL_{+}=-\partial_{x}{\mathcal{L}}_{+}\partial_{x}, where ℒ+=−∂x2−ω−∂x−2−p|ϕ′|p−2ϕ′{\mathcal{L}}_{+}=-\partial_{x}^{2}-\omega-\partial_{x}^{-2}-p|\phi^{\prime}|^{p-2}\phi^{\prime}, D⁡(ℒ+)=H2​(ℝ)∩H˙−2​(ℝ)D({\mathcal{L}}_{+})=H^{2}(\mathbb{R})\cap\dot{H}^{-2}(\mathbb{R}).

In terms of the new operator μzx=−∂xℒ+zx\mu z_{x}=-\partial_{x}{\mathcal{L}}_{+}z_{x}. Since the function spaces require vanishing at both infinities, this is equivalent to μz=−ℒ+∂xz\mu z=-{\mathcal{L}}_{+}\partial_{x}z or μ\mu is an eigenvalue for −ℒ+∂x-{\mathcal{L}}_{+}\partial_{x}. Equivalently, μ¯\bar{\mu} is an eigenvalue for the adjoint ∂xℒ+=(−ℒ+∂x)∗\partial_{x}{\mathcal{L}}_{+}=(-{\mathcal{L}}_{+}\partial_{x})^{*} or ∂xℒ+​z=μ¯​z\partial_{x}{\mathcal{L}}_{+}z=\bar{\mu}z. Clearly, since ℜ⁡μ=ℜ⁡μ¯\Re\mu=\Re\bar{\mu}, the spectral stability of the traveling wave ϕ⁡(x−ω​t)\phi(x-\omega t) is equivalent to the following eigenvalue problem

(1.16) ∂xℒ+​z=λ​z\partial_{x}{\mathcal{L}}_{+}z=\lambda z

not having non-trivial solutions (λ,z),ℜ⁡λ>0,z≠0(\lambda,z),\Re\lambda>0,z\neq 0.

For future reference, we introduce two notions of non-degeneracy of ϕ\phi, which are generically expected to hold.

Definition 1.

We say that the wave ϕ\phi is non-degenerate, if K​e​r​[ℒ+]=s​p​a​n​[ϕ′]Ker[{\mathcal{L}}_{+}]=span[\phi^{\prime}]. We say that the wave ϕ\phi is weakly non-degenerate, if ϕ⟂K​e​r​[ℒ+]\phi\perp Ker[{\mathcal{L}}_{+}].

Remark: Clearly a non-degenerate wave is weakly non-degenerate, but not vice versa. For weakly non-degenerate waves, the important quantity ℒ+−1​ϕ{\mathcal{L}}_{+}^{-1}\phi is well-defined.

Theorem 2.

Let 1<p<31<p<3 and λ>0\lambda>0. Then, the constrained minimizers ϕλ\phi_{\lambda} for (1.9), constructed in Theorem 1 are weakly non-degenerate in the sense of Definition 1. In particular, ℒ+−1​ϕλ{\mathcal{L}}_{+}^{-1}\phi_{\lambda} is well-defined. Under the condition

(1.17) ⟨ℒ+−1​ϕ,ϕ⟩≠0,\langle{\mathcal{L}}_{+}^{-1}\phi,\phi\rangle\neq 0,

the waves ϕλ\phi_{\lambda} are spectrally stable. That is, the eigenvalue problem (1.16) does not support non-trivial solutions (λ,z):ℜ⁡λ>0,z≠0(\lambda,z):\Re\lambda>0,z\neq 0. Similar result holds for limit waves of (1.9).

For 1<p<51<p<5 and λ>0\lambda>0, let ϕλ\phi_{\lambda} be a constrained minimizer for (1.12). Then, again ϕλ\phi_{\lambda} are weakly non-degenerate and under (1.17), they are spectrally stable as well. Same statement applies to the limit waves.

Remark: The condition (1.17) is a commonly imposed technical condition in the literature. In fact, it guarantees that the zero eigenvalue for ∂xℒ+\partial_{x}{\mathcal{L}}_{+} has an algebraic multiplicity of exactly two, see Proposition 6 below.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we state some preliminary results and background information - most of these are well-known or standard, yet others, like Proposition 2 require quite a bit of analysis. Section 3 contains the main variational construction, which proceeds through compensated compactness arguments. The argument here requires a surprising detailed, hands on Fourier analytic methods in order to verify the subadditivity of the cost functional. In addition, Euler-Lagrange equations are derived and some basic spectral properties of the linearized operators are verified as well. In Section 4, we present the basics of the instability index count theory, along with some corollaries, which fit our situation well. In addition, we establish a general framework, which yields the spectral stability of the waves, Lemma 8. This is then easily applied to the previously waves to infer their spectral stability.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Weak solutions and bootstrapping regularity

In our considerations, we will need to rely, at least initially, on a weak solution formulations of certain elliptic PDE’s, specifically (1.8). More concretely,

Definition 2.

We say that g∈H2​(ℝ)g\in H^{2}(\mathbb{R}) is a weak solution of the equation

2.2. Exponential decay of the waves and eigenfunctions

In this section, we show that the solutions to the elliptic profile equations (1.8) have exponential decay at ±∞\pm\infty, and in fact we are able to compute explicitly the leading order terms. Similar result holds for any element in the kernels of the linearized operators ℒ+,L+{\mathcal{L}}_{+},L_{+}. The precise result is as follows.

then

3. Variational construction

In this section, we provide the variational construction of the waves. It turns out that for some aspects of the construction, it is more beneficial to look at the following alternative ℐ,𝒥\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J} defined in the beginning. Introduce the following functions, which are the corresponding infimums, if they exists, of the constrained minimization problems

(3.1) mI​(λ)=infu∈H2,‖ux‖2=λ{12​∫ℝ|ux​x|2+|u|2​𝑑x−1p+1​∫ℝ|ux|p​ux​𝑑x},\displaystyle m_{I}(\lambda)=\inf_{u\in H^{2},\left\|u_{x}\right\|^{2}=\lambda}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|u_{xx}|^{2}+|u|^{2}dx-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|u_{x}|^{p}u_{x}dx\right\},

(3.3) mℐ​(λ)=infU∈H1∩H˙−1,‖U‖2=λ{12​∫ℝ|Ux|2+|∂x−1U|2​𝑑x−1p+1​∫ℝ|U|p​U​𝑑x},\displaystyle m_{\mathcal{I}}(\lambda)=\inf_{U\in H^{1}\cap\dot{H}^{-1},\left\|U\right\|^{2}=\lambda}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|U_{x}|^{2}+|\partial^{-1}_{x}U|^{2}dx-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|U|^{p}Udx\right\},

These are usually referred to as cost functions. We have the following sequence of lemmas, that establishes some important properties of the functionals and the mm functions.

3.3. Existence of the waves

Proposition 3.

Let 1<p<31<p<3. Then, the minimization problem (3.1) has a solution. For 1<p<51<p<5, the minimization problem (3.2) has a solution.

4. Stability of the waves

We start this section by developing the necessary general tools, which imply stability of the waves under consideration. Most of the content in Section 4.1 is contained in some recent papers, but we summarize it for the reader’s convenience. Note that our reasoning applies equally well to both the fourth order and the second order versions of the eigenvalue problems, see (1.15), (1.16).

4.1. Instability index theory

In this section, we present the instability index count theory, specifically applied to eigenvalue problems in the form (1.16). As we have previously discussed, the main issue is whether or nor, the eigenvalue problem (1.16) has non-trivial solutions (μ,z)(\mu,z). To that end, we mostly follow the theory developed in [8], in the specific case when the self-adjoint operator is 𝒥=∂x\mathcal{J}=\partial_{x}. More specifically, consider a (slightly more general) eigenvalue problem

(4.1) ∂xℒ​z=μ​z,\partial_{x}{\mathcal{L}}z=\mu z,

4.4. The proof of Theorem 2

The proof of Theorem 2 consists of applying Lemma 8 to ℋ=ℒ+\mathcal{H}={\mathcal{L}}_{+} and ξ0:=λ−1/2ϕλ\xi_{0}:=\lambda^{-1/2}\phi_{\lambda}.
